greek.title: The Slave Who Shaped Citizens
greek.body:
The paidagōgos occupied a peculiar position in the Athenian household: neither parent nor teacher, yet charged with a boy's moral formation. Typically an older slave, often foreign-born, he walked his young charge through the streets to the grammatistes for letters, the kitharistes for music, the paidotribes for wrestling. His authority was real. He could rebuke, restrain, even punish. Plato's Lysis shows such a man forbidding his ward from driving the family chariot.

The relationship bred intimacy. Boys spent more waking hours with their paidagōgoi than with their fathers. Some remained loyal companions into adulthood. Yet the role carried ambiguity: this trusted guide, this shaper of future citizens, remained property. The word itself migrated, shedding its servile origins to mean any educator, a transformation that erased the uncomfortable truth at its heart.
